We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-4637)
response:
Quantization-aware training (QAT) embeds fake quantization nodes during training so the model learns to tolerate discretization error, but the calibration dataset used to set scale factors and zero-points implicitly encodes an assumption about the activation distribution the model will encounter at deployment. When the deployment distribution diverges from the calibration distribution — a domain shift, a new user population, longer input sequences — scale factors tuned to calibration statistics become miscalibrated: activations that were rare outliers during calibration become modal at deployment, and the clipped dynamic range introduces systematic bias rather than random rounding noise. The outlier channel problem sharpens this: in transformer models, a small number of activation channels (often 0.1–1% of channels) carry disproportionate magnitude — LLM.int8() (Dettmers et al., 2022) showed that these outlier channels emerge suddenly at ~6.7B parameters and are highly input-dependent, meaning calibration data that doesn't excite them will produce scale factors that catastrophically clip real deployment values. The accuracy cliff is the non-linearity experts dread most: perplexity or task accuracy degrades gracefully through INT8, then drops precipitously at INT4 or below because the quantization grid becomes too coarse to represent the outlier channel magnitudes without overflow or clipping, and the effective information bottleneck is no longer additive noise but structured erasure of high-salience features. A beginner assumes that more calibration data is always better and that the QAT loss curve is the right diagnostic; an expert knows that calibration set coverage of the outlier activation regime matters more than size, and that smooth training loss can mask latent miscalibration that only surfaces as a deployment cliff when bit-width drops below a threshold that was never probed during development.

Since both AWQ and GPTQ failures ultimately trace back to calibration set mismatch, what would a theoretically principled calibration set selection criterion look like — and is activation kurtosis matching, Hessian coverage, or something else the right objective to optimize?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-4640)
response:
A theoretically principled calibration criterion should minimize the expected quantization error under the deployment distribution, which decomposes into two distinct objectives that are in tension: covering the support of the activation distribution (so no deployment activation falls outside the calibration-observed dynamic range) and weighting samples by their Hessian contribution (so rounding decisions are optimized for high-leverage activation directions). Kurtosis matching alone is insufficient because kurtosis is a marginal statistic — it captures the tail heaviness of individual channel distributions but ignores the joint activation structure across channels, and GPTQ's Hessian encodes precisely this joint structure; two calibration sets with identical per-channel kurtosis can produce radically different Hessians if their token co-occurrence patterns differ. The most principled existing formulation comes from the Fisher information perspective: the optimal calibration set is one whose empirical Fisher (computed over quantization perturbations) approximates the deployment Fisher, which is equivalent to saying the calibration set should induce the same curvature landscape over weight space as deployment data — this is the implicit criterion that QuIP# (Tseng et al., 2024) gestures toward with its incoherence preprocessing, which randomizes the activation basis to make the Hessian more uniform and reduce sensitivity to any particular calibration set. A practical approximation to this ideal is activation subspace coverage: using SVD on the calibration activation matrix per layer and checking that the top-
𝑘
k singular vectors span the same subspace as deployment activations, since Hessian eigenstructure is dominated by the principal activation directions (Yao et al., 2022, ZeroQuant); this is more actionable than kurtosis matching and directly predicts GPTQ failure modes. The uncomfortable conclusion is that for a truly unknown deployment distribution, no fixed calibration set is optimal — the right answer is either online recalibration (updating scale factors or rounding decisions as deployment data accumulates, as in adaptive quantization schemes like LUT-GEMM) or deliberately constructing a calibration set that over-represents high-kurtosis, high-magnitude activation regimes relative to their natural frequency, accepting some calibration-time suboptimality to buy robustness against distribution tail events.

response:
The unknown-deployment-Fisher problem fundamentally undermines one-shot PTQ's theoretical guarantees: PTQ is solving a proxy optimization problem whose objective diverges from the true objective by an amount proportional to the Fisher discrepancy between calibration and deployment distributions, and this discrepancy is unbounded in the worst case — meaning PTQ accuracy guarantees are vacuous under arbitrary distribution shift, a point made precise by Nagel et al. (2020, "Up or Down? Adaptive Rounding for Post-Training Quantization") who show that ADAROUND's optimality proof holds only when calibration activations are drawn from the same distribution as inference. The closest thing to a formal bound comes from framing PTQ-versus-QAT as a domain adaptation problem: the quantization error gap between PTQ and QAT is lower-bounded by the H-divergence between calibration and deployment activation distributions (Ben-David et al., 2010 transfer learning framework applied to quantization by Zhong et al., 2023), which means that for well-separated domains the gap cannot be closed by any PTQ algorithm regardless of how sophisticated its rounding criterion is — QAT's advantage is precisely that it optimizes over the model parameters rather than just the quantization parameters, giving it a strictly larger solution space. Iterative quantization schemes that observe deployment feedback — such as online quantization error correction or deployment-time scale factor adaptation — are theoretically superior but face a practical trilemma: the feedback signal requires either labeled deployment data (unavailable), unsupervised proxy losses (noisy), or storing full-precision weights for online fine-tuning (expensive); QuaRot (Ashkboos et al., 2024) partially addresses this by rotating weight matrices to reduce outlier sensitivity without needing deployment data, effectively reducing the H-divergence sensitivity of the PTQ solution. Empirically, the PTQ-QAT gap at INT4 is substantial: on LLaMA-2-7B, GPTQ achieves ~5.5 perplexity on WikiText-2 versus ~4.8 for full precision, while QAT-based methods like LLM-QAT (Liu et al., 2023) recover to ~5.1 — a gap that widens further under domain shift because PTQ's fixed rounding decisions compound with the distributional error whereas QAT's learned fake-quantization nodes adapt the model's internal representations to absorb quantization noise more robustly. The practical implication is that one-shot PTQ is viable only when the operator can bound the deployment distribution shift — essentially treating PTQ as appropriate for near-distribution serving and QAT (or hybrid schemes with deployment-time recalibration) as necessary for open-ended deployment, a distinction the field has been slow to formalize but which is increasingly apparent in production LLM serving systems that observe accuracy cliffs on user queries outside the calibration domain.

Runtime-adaptive quantization grids exist on a spectrum from fully dynamic (recomputing scale factors per-tensor per-token) to block-adaptive (updating scales every 
𝐵
B tokens), and the fully dynamic end is actually already implemented in LLM.int8() which computes per-row and per-column absmax scales on-the-fly for every matrix multiply — the reason this works at INT8 but becomes impractical at INT4 is that INT8's 256-level grid tolerates the approximation error introduced by computing scales from a single token's activation vector, whereas INT4's 16-level grid requires scale factors accurate enough that single-sample absmax estimates introduce quantization error that exceeds the grid spacing itself. The fundamental compute overhead of fully dynamic scaling is a reduction operation over the activation tensor before every GEMM, which adds roughly 10–15% latency on modern GPUs for large matrix sizes (measured in FlashAttention-style kernel profiling) and — more critically — breaks the fused kernel optimizations that make static-scale INT4 GEMMs fast: CUTLASS and Triton INT4 kernels achieve high throughput by assuming scale factors are loaded from L2 cache once per tile, and making them input-dependent forces a synchronization barrier that destroys the memory access pattern. The memory overhead is less about storing scales (per-channel scales for a 70B model add only ~1MB) and more about the bandwidth cost: dynamic scales must be computed in a separate pass and streamed alongside weight tiles, effectively doubling the memory transactions for scale data and reducing the effective memory bandwidth utilization that INT4 quantization was trying to recover in the first place. Atom (Zhao et al., 2024) represents the most practical compromise: it uses a fine-grained static grid (group size 128) combined with per-token dynamic activation scales, achieving most of the robustness of fully dynamic quantization at roughly 20% overhead over static INT4 by exploiting the observation that weight scales can remain static while activation scales need to adapt — this works because weight outliers are fixed by model structure but activation outliers are input-dependent. The fundamental constraint that makes true runtime adaptivity impractical at scale is the causality-latency tradeoff: to set a scale factor that covers the full activation range for a given token, you must observe the full activation vector before quantizing it, which in autoregressive generation means you cannot pipeline quantization with the preceding computation without introducing a bubble equal to the reduction latency, and at batch sizes of 512+ tokens this bubble compounds across all layers to add tens of milliseconds of non-parallelizable serial work per generated token.
